title: Easy exam 14
about: Ten single-choice questions on the basics: init systems, functions, standard streams, absolute paths, escaping in grep, job control, variable names, the mode string, crontab fields and chaining commands.

questions.title: Init systems
questions.text: Which statement about init systems is TRUE?

options.t: `launchd` is the init system of macOS.
options.why: Linux distributions mostly use `systemd`, older ones used SysV `init`, and macOS uses `launchd`.

options.t: `systemd` is the init system of macOS.
options.why: `systemd` is the standard on Linux; macOS uses `launchd`.

options.t: SysV `init` describes the services as unit files and starts them in parallel.
options.why: Unit files are a `systemd` idea; SysV init runs the scripts of `/etc/init.d` in order, by runlevel.

options.t: The BSD systems use `systemd` as their init by default.
options.why: The BSDs have their own, simpler init.

questions.title: A function with a parameter
questions.text: A script contains `greet() { echo "Hi $1"; }` followed by the two lines `greet Ana` and `greet`. What does it print?

options.t: `Hi Ana` and then `Hi `
options.why: Inside the function `$1` is its first argument; in the second call there is none, so `$1` is empty.

options.t: `Hi Ana` twice
options.why: The second call has no argument: `$1` does not keep the value of the first call.

options.t: `Hi Ana` and then an error, because the function needs an argument.
options.why: Bash does not check arguments: a missing one is just empty.

options.t: Nothing, because the function is defined but never called.
options.why: The two following lines are the calls.

questions.title: The three streams
questions.text: Which line gives the standard streams with their numbers and their defaults?

options.t: stdin is 0 (the keyboard), stdout is 1 (the screen) and stderr is 2 (the screen).
options.why: In `2> errors.txt` the number 2 selects the standard error.

options.t: stdin is 1 (the keyboard), stdout is 2 (the screen) and stderr is 3 (the screen).
options.why: The numbering starts at 0.

options.t: stdin is 0 (the screen), stdout is 1 (the keyboard) and stderr is 2 (a log file).
options.why: The input comes from the keyboard and both outputs go to the screen by default.

options.t: stdin is 2 (the keyboard), stdout is 1 (the screen) and stderr is 0 (the screen).
options.why: The numbers of stdin and stderr are swapped.

questions.title: What makes a path absolute
questions.text: Which statement defines an absolute path?

options.t: A path that starts at the root directory, so it begins with `/`.
options.why: It means the same wherever you are, for example `/etc/passwd`.

options.t: A path that starts at the current directory, such as `./notes`.
options.why: That is a relative path.

options.t: A path that has no `..` in it.
options.why: `docs/notes` has none and is still relative; `/home/../etc` has one and is still absolute.

options.t: A path of more than one component, such as `docs/notes`.
options.why: The number of components is irrelevant: what matters is the first `/`.

questions.title: Escaping a dot
questions.text: The file has the lines `axb` and `a.b`. Which statement about searching for a literal dot is FALSE?

options.t: `grep 'a\.b' file` prints only `a.b`.
options.why: True: inside quotes the backslash reaches `grep`, which then reads the dot as an ordinary character.

options.t: `grep -F a.b file` prints only `a.b`.
options.why: True: `-F` treats the pattern as a fixed string, with no special characters.

options.t: `grep 'a[.]b' file` prints only `a.b`.
options.why: True: inside brackets the dot is an ordinary character.

options.t: `grep a\.b file`, without quotes, prints only `a.b`.
options.why: False: the shell removes the backslash first, so `grep` receives `a.b` and prints both lines.

questions.title: Suspending a job
questions.text: Which statement about `Ctrl+C` and `Ctrl+Z` is FALSE?

options.t: `Ctrl+C` sends `SIGINT` to the foreground job, which normally ends.
options.why: True.

options.t: `Ctrl+Z` stops the foreground job and gives the prompt back.
options.why: True: the job is suspended, not finished.

options.t: A job stopped with `Ctrl+Z` can be resumed with `fg` or `bg`.
options.why: True: `fg` in the foreground and `bg` in the background.

options.t: A job stopped with `Ctrl+Z` is terminated, and its memory is freed.
options.why: False: it stays in memory in the stopped state until it is resumed or killed.

questions.title: Spaces around the equals sign
questions.text: You type `count = 5` in bash. What happens?

options.t: The shell tries to run a command called `count` with the arguments `=` and `5`, and answers "command not found".
options.why: In an assignment there must be no spaces around `=`.

options.t: The variable `count` is set to `5`.
options.why: That is what `count=5`, with no spaces, does.

options.t: The variable `count` is set to the string ` 5`, with a leading space.
options.why: The shell does not treat the line as an assignment at all.

options.t: The shell prints `5`, the value of the assignment.
options.why: Assignments print nothing in the shell.

questions.title: The mode string
questions.text: Which command prints the mode string, such as `-rw-r--r--`, of the file `notes.txt`?

options.t: `ls -l notes.txt`
options.why: The long format starts with the type and the permissions of owner, group and others.

options.t: `ls notes.txt`
options.why: It prints only the name of the file.

options.t: `ls -i notes.txt`
options.why: It prints the inode number followed by the name.

options.t: `cat -l notes.txt`
options.why: `cat` shows the content of the file and has no `-l` option.

questions.title: A crontab line
questions.text: Which statement about the crontab line `30 3 * * 1-5 /usr/bin/backup` is TRUE?

options.t: The command runs at 03:30 from Monday to Friday.
options.why: The fields are minute, hour, day of the month, month and day of the week.

options.t: The command runs at 03:30 on the days 1 to 5 of every month.
options.why: The range `1-5` is in the fifth field, which is the day of the week.

options.t: The command runs every 30 minutes during the hours 3 to 5.
options.why: `30` is the minute field and `3` the hour field; they are not intervals.

options.t: The command runs at 30:03 every weekday.
options.why: Hours go from 0 to 23 and minutes from 0 to 59.

questions.title: Running a command only after another
questions.text: Which line creates the directory `d` and goes into it only if the creation succeeded?

options.t: `mkdir d && cd d`
options.why: `&&` runs the second command only when the first one ends with status 0.

options.t: `mkdir d ; cd d`
options.why: `;` runs `cd` whatever happened to `mkdir`.

options.t: `mkdir d || cd d`
options.why: `||` runs `cd` only when `mkdir` failed.

options.t: `mkdir d & cd d`
options.why: `&` runs `mkdir` in the background, so `cd` may run before the directory exists.
